paras: The lynching of Bud Johnson was the burning to death of a Black man by a mob in western Florida in March 1919, after he was taken from a sheriff's party at Castleberry while being moved away from the Pensacola jail. Johnson had been accused of attacking a white woman at Pace, Florida, and was burned near the scene of the alleged crime. The case drew wide attention in the Black press after the NAACP published Governor Sidney J. Catts's reply to its protest, in which he wrote that the lynchers could not be brought to trial in Florida.

According to a Pensacola dispatch, Johnson, described as "Colored," was accused of attacking "a well-known white woman" at Pace, and officers said he had admitted the attack. Sheriff Harwell, spelled Harvell in other texts, captured him and brought him to Pensacola by launch on a Wednesday night, where he was placed in the jail. Catts later wrote that he had been called at midnight, told of the crime, and had the man carried to the Pensacola jail.

On Thursday night a crowd of more than a thousand people gathered around the Pensacola jail and demanded the prisoner. As mob violence became apparent, the sheriff removed Johnson and hurried him by automobile toward Castleberry, which the Cleveland Advocate placed in Alabama, hoping to board a fast train for Montgomery. By the governor's account, the sheriff had telephoned that morning to say the prisoner was not safe, and Catts ordered him taken to Montgomery and then sent to Jacksonville for safekeeping.

When the crowd learned that Johnson had been taken away, several fast automobiles were commandeered, and the sheriff's party was overtaken near the Florida state line early Friday, March 14. Johnson was carried back to the scene of the alleged crime, identified by the woman, and burned to death. The mob then dispersed, and the dispatch reported everything quiet. Catts described the killing as death "at the hands of an infuriated mob from Santa Rosa County."

On March 15 the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, through its secretary John R. Shillady, telegraphed Catts about the lynchings of Johnson and of Joe Walker, killed by a mob in a separate case near Madison, and asked that the lynchers be brought to justice. In his reply of March 18, Catts said he had tried to keep down lynching but that, when a white woman was assaulted, trying those who saw that the accused met death was impossible because "the citizenship will not stand for it." He blamed "the roving, transient, irresponsible and unmarried element of tramp negroes" and urged the association to teach Black people instead of offering "maudlin sympathy."

Shillady answered on March 28, commending the attempt to safeguard the prisoner but calling it a serious commentary on Florida's laws that a governor would apologize for burnings at the stake. He also answered the governor's call for education by citing the gap between Florida's per capita school spending on white and Black children. No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The first Black-press reports, on March 22 in the Cleveland Advocate, the Dallas Express and the Ohio State Monitor, were Pensacola wire briefs that repeated the officers' statement that Johnson had confessed. The Monitor ran the item as "Negro Burned to Death," with the subhead "Had Admitted Attacking White Woman at Pace, Fla." By contrast, the Wisconsin Weekly Blade added that "the usual tale that 'the Negro confessed' was handed out by the white press associations and papers," wording the Phoenix Tribune repeated in May.

The Catts-Shillady correspondence gave the case a second life in April, appearing in the St. Louis Argus as "Cannot Bring Mob Leaders to Trial Says Gov.," in the Ohio State Monitor as "Florida Governor Defends Lynching," and in the Dallas Express and the Chicago Defender. The Monitor's editorial "Gov. Catts and Mob Ridden Florida" said that "the Governor of Florida takes his stand with the mob" and contrasted his phrase "negro brute, or a white man." The letter remained a reference point into the summer: a Jacksonville reader attacked it in the Defender's mail column, and the Washington Bee cited it in a report on the riot at Millen, Georgia.

In July the Richmond Planet included the case, as "Judge Johnson" burned at the stake at Castleberry on March 4, in an editorial list of the year's burnings since President Wilson's appeal against mob rule.

Accounts differ on where Johnson was being sent: the wire named the Jackson County jail at Marianna by way of Montgomery, while Catts wrote that he had ordered him sent through Montgomery to Jacksonville. The place is also given variously as Castleberry, Alabama, as Castleberry, Florida, and, in the governor's letter, as "the one at Milton," though the wire placed the burning near Pace. The Planet's date of March 4 and the name "Judge Johnson" conflict with the contemporary wire, dated March 14, and with every other report. The confession rests only on the word of officers, which the Blade rejected.

reader.title: Lynching of Bud Johnson
bases: A mob took Johnson from a sheriff's party and burned him to death near the scene of an alleged attack on a white woman (A1, A3, A10).

A mob that had gathered by the thousand at the Pensacola jail overtook the sheriff's party in several automobiles, seized Johnson and burned him to death over an accusation of attacking a white woman (A1, A3); the governor himself called it a death 'at the hands of an infuriated mob' (A10).
The Pensacola wire reports (A1, A2, A3) are confirmed in their core by Governor Catts's independent letter, which says Sheriff Harvell was overtaken and the prisoner killed by a mob (A10).

Papers ran the Catts-Shillady exchange under headlines such as 'Florida Governor Defends Lynching' and 'Cannot Bring Mob Leaders to Trial Says Gov.'
